paras: The threatened lynching of Harper Meadows was a reported plan in February 1888 by citizens of Decker township, Illinois, to take Meadows from the jail at Fairfield and lynch him for the killing of Joseph F. Leavers. No report shows the mob reached the jail, and two months later Meadows was convicted of the murder and sentenced to fifty years in the penitentiary. The Olney dispatch announcing the mob ran in papers in Indiana, Tennessee, West Virginia, Kansas and Arkansas.

On Saturday night, February 11, 1888, Joseph F. Leaver, described as a bridegroom of a week, was killed by a shotgun blast fired through a window while he sat at his fireside about twenty miles southwest of Olney. The same shot slightly wounded his 17-year-old brother-in-law, Washington Osterman, while Leaver's wife and her mother escaped injury. Harper Meadows, 21, who had unsuccessfully sought Miss Osterman's hand, was arrested on suspicion.

According to a St. Louis dispatch, Mrs. Leaver stated that she had rejected Meadows's offer of marriage and that he had then threatened to dispose of the man who married her. The statement "aroused strong feeling against him," and with Meadows, said to come from "a highly respected family of the neighborhood," held in the Fairfield jail, the people were reported "in a state of high excitement."

In a dispatch dated February 14, Olney reported that word had arrived the previous evening that "a large number of citizens of Decker township" were organizing a mob to go to Fairfield and lynch Meadows. The men were expected to reach the jail before daylight, and the dispatch predicted that, being "reliable and determined men," they would "execute swift vengeance on the murderer." No account of the mob arriving at the jail, of a confrontation with officers, or of the plan being abandoned appears in the coverage.

Meadows was tried at Fairfield and, according to an Indiana weekly's news summary of April 11, was convicted of the murder of Joseph Leavers the previous Friday and given fifty years in the penitentiary. The Ohio Democrat carried the same brief three days later.

The coverage came entirely from white papers relaying Illinois dispatches, and none of it mentioned the race of anyone involved. The Olney dispatch treated Meadows's guilt as settled, calling him "the young man who assassinated" Leavers days before any trial, and described the would-be lynchers with approval. The Indianapolis Journal headed it "Lynching Threatened," the Memphis Appeal "Another Lynching Talked Of," and the Wheeling Daily Intelligencer "A Lynching Mob Organized," the last changing the closing words to "swift justice on Meadows."

The story kept circulating after its news value had passed. The Nicodemus Cyclone in Kansas printed it on February 24 under "Lynchers at Work," directly above a report of the hanging of Alonzo Holly, described as "a negro," by a mob at the Pinkneyville jail. The Forrest City Times in Arkansas ran a one-sentence version on March 3 and again on March 10, still in the present tense of a mob about to set out. Papers that reported the killing and arrest, such as the Fort Worth Daily Gazette and the Mower County Transcript, did not mention the mob, and the brief trial notices did not mention the threat.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of Harper Meadows
bases: A mob was reported organizing to take Meadows from the Fairfield jail and lynch him (A3); no report shows it carried out the attempt.

A 'large number' of Decker township citizens were said to be organizing to lynch Meadows for the Leavers killing (A3), but no one was killed: Meadows was later tried and sentenced to fifty years (A11, A12). It was a threatened lynching only.
The mob report comes from one Olney dispatch, reprinted in several papers (A3, A5, A6, A7, A9); the killing, arrest and conviction are reported separately (A1, A2, A11).

accounts.label: Olney dispatch (mob report)
accounts.gist: Citizens of Decker township were organizing a mob to go to Fairfield and lynch Meadows before daylight; as 'reliable and determined men' they would carry it out.

accounts.label: St. Louis dispatch (arrest)
accounts.gist: Meadows was arrested on suspicion after Mrs. Leaver's statement and held at Fairfield amid 'high excitement'.

accounts.label: Trial report
accounts.gist: Meadows was convicted of the murder at Fairfield and sentenced to fifty years.

framing.detail: The Olney dispatch treated Meadows's guilt as settled ('the young man who assassinated') and the mob approvingly as 'reliable and determined men' who would 'execute swift vengeance on the murderer'.

Out-of-state papers ran the dispatch under headlines such as 'Another Lynching Talked Of', 'A Lynching Mob Organized' and 'Lynchers at Work', some changing the closing words to 'swift justice on Meadows'.

conflicts.note: Spelling varies by dispatch; the earliest Olney report uses Leaver, the mob and trial reports Leavers.

conflicts.field: when word of the mob reached Olney
conflicts.note: The Forrest City brief is a late condensed rewrite; the dated Olney dispatch is the better evidence.
